data.title: Trump calls Nvidia CEO to talk AI — and gets put on speakerphone in all-hands meeting
data.description: President Donald Trump on Monday called Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during a company all-hands meeting and gave another full-throated defense of artificial intelligence after Huang put the call on speakerphone. Trump characterized concerns about AI safety as a “hoax,” while telling Huang that the U.S. had to beat China in AI innovation and development. “The robots will not be taking over. The AI will not be taking over the rest of the world. The whole thing is a hoax,” Trump said, suggesting that critics are “just playing right into the hands of a lot of people that don’t want to see it happen. That could be political people, that could also be China.” Trump also lauded politically unpopular data centers, calling them “great” and saying they make people and states “wealthy.” “It’s the oil of the next 20, 25 years, it’s bigger than the internet and AI, you know, much more so,” he said, while adding that people “have to be a little careful” and do things “prudently.” A video of Trump’s call, posted on X, was reposted by the Trump War Room account, which is associated with a Trump-aligned PAC. The call is also included in a podcast that Huang was recording at the time. Nvidia said it had no comment on Huang’s exchange with Trump or whether they will be meeting soon to discuss these issues. Trump’s comments to Nvidia, one of the world’s biggest manufacturers of AI chips and hardware, come as AI leaders have called for slowing down development of the technology. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in an essay over the weekend that AI development needed safeguards, which was quickly endorsed by Tesla CEO Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, among others. It came after last week researchers at leading AI companies stepped down from their jobs and spoke out over safety concerns, some describing them as an existential threat to humanity. Former President Barack Obama urged Democrats last week to prioritize the development of an AI agenda. Trump, however, has firmly stood by his support for AI development. In a flurry of social media posts Monday, Trump described AI concerns as a “SICK conspiracy” and a “hoax.” During the Nvidia phone call, Trump said he assumed Huang was on the same page as him regarding AI development; Huang said they were. “We’re going to make sure that everybody wins in the AI race in America. Every industry, every company, every state, every people,” he told Trump during their call. The Nvidia CEO, who helped persuade Trump last year to not send National Guard troops to San Francisco, sits on Trump’s council of science and technology advisers. He has lobbied lawmakers to allow sales of Nvidia around the world, which lawmakers have said could advantage China and undercut U.S. leadership in technology. His conversation with Trump came as House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who had been urged by House Democrats to end recess early so the lower chamber could take legislative action regarding AI safety, said this week that industry leaders should be the ones taking the lead on safety. Johnson said Monday that Trump would call a meeting with AI leaders. A source familiar with the matter told NBC News that a meeting between Trump and the leaders was “in the works,” but no clear timing had been nailed down.

data.title: Trump says AI doesn’t need guardrails, only a ‘high IQ’ president
data.description: President Donald Trump rejected the idea of placing guardrails on artificial intelligence, saying in a Truth Social post Monday that the only control needed is “a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” In the same post, he appeared to hint at the government pursuing criminal or regulatory penalties against AI companies after industry insiders warned of potentially catastrophic dangers posed by the rapidly evolving technology. “The Trump Administration has stopped AI ‘people’ from doing bad, or potentially bad, ‘things,’ like Dario (Anthropic!), who is now pretending to be a ‘perfect little angel’ — and we will continue to do so!” he said, referring to Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI chatbot. Amodei said in a Saturday essay that AI companies should “slow the pace” of AI development. “We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies!” Trump continued. “There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so. Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers, BEWARE!” Even as the American public and members of his own party grow increasingly skeptical of AI, the president has framed the technology’s continued growth as an economic and geopolitical imperative. Communities that reject AI data centers will wind up “backwards and poor,” he warned recently. And in Ireland last weekend, he was even blunter: “Whoever wins AI wins.” Yet, a recent NBC News Decision Desk poll found that 70% of adults said they were more worried about AI than excited about it. A similar percentage — 69% of adults — said they somewhat or strongly oppose the construction of an AI data center in their local area. That includes 57% of Republican voters. Trump remained undeterred Monday afternoon, returning to Truth Social in a full-throated defense of AI, saying that “AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX.” In the same post, he said that AI would be “the Greatest Economic Development Engine in History — Bigger than Oil, Gold, Diamonds, or even the Internet.” Amodei’s recent warning has prompted other AI leaders to publicly call for a slowdown in its development so researchers can better understand and control any threats posed by the technology. They include OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who said his company would adopt one of the safeguards Amodei proposed in his essay. Last week, Anthropic AI researcher Jacob Coxon resigned, writing in a viral X post that OpenAI and Anthropic were “gambling with our lives,” warning that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” A lead Anthropic researcher, Evan Hubinger, said in a post on X that Coxon was right, saying, “we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Many politicians responded with their own calls for stronger checks on AI to address safety concerns. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., on Monday called for a Senate briefing with top administration officials, while House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said he expects Trump to “summon” AI platform leaders for a “deliberate discussion about the responsibility of the companies to maintain safety and what role, if any, the government has to play in that.” A meeting between Trump and AI leaders is “in the works,” but no timing has been nailed down yet, a source familiar with the matter told NBC News. Beijing on Monday disparaged the warnings from U.S. tech leaders as “fearmongering” from a “Cold War playbook” aimed at hobbling China. Vice President JD Vance on Monday told reporters that AI leaders’ warnings is “something that we’re concerned by,” but said the administration wants to ensure “we actually regulate smartly.” “I have to say, just personally, I feel a little bit weird about the fact that you have so many frontier AI tech companies kind of coming to the government and begging the government to regulate them,” Vance said. “It feels a little bit to me like a bit of a Trojan horse. So I think we just have to be careful about this.” During his trip to Ireland, Trump asserted over the weekend that the U.S. was leading China on artificial intelligence and said that “whoever wins AI wins.” “We can put guardrails,” he said Sunday. “We can do this and that, but I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn’t be bringing it up, and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen.”

data.title: China dismisses AI slowdown calls and blasts ‘fearmongering’ from U.S. tech leaders
data.description: HONG KONG — Urgent calls for a slowdown in the development of artificial intelligence may cite a grave threat to humanity, but China says the warnings are instead aimed at slowing its progress as America’s rival superpower. Beijing on Monday dismissed the intervention from U.S. tech leaders as “fearmongering” and part of a “Cold War playbook.” It’s the latest sign that competition between the two countries could outweigh mounting safety concerns, after President Donald Trump also rebuffed the warnings from industry leaders and said his focus was on beating China on AI. The comments followed a lengthy essay that was published Saturday by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX founder Elon Musk. Amodei said that companies should deliberately “slow the pace” at which they improve their models given the potential risks. He also said that a “Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the United States and the world,” and called for the U.S. to restrict sales of key tech to China. That message was not welcomed by Beijing. “Fearmongering, confrontation and malicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance and serve no one’s interests,” China’s foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters at a regular news briefing on Monday. The state-run Global Times newspaper had a more blunt tone on Sunday, blasting the call for an industry-wide slowdown as “packed with containment provisions targeting China and is, in essence, a ‘Cold War playbook’ for the AI sector.” AI has advanced at a breakneck speed, with models rapidly getting smarter, faster and cheaper. They have also frequently outpaced technical safeguards, fueling security fears. Those fears have now reached a crescendo, but also exposed just how far apart Beijing and Washington seem to be on cooperating to address them. Amodei himself likened the situation to the Cold War arms race, telling CBS’ ‘Sunday Morning’ that the two sides should work together, but that he didn’t hold out much hope. Altman, the head of OpenAI, similarly said on X late Sunday that “where we will need the help of our government is for international coordination.” But that might not be compatible with Trump’s approach. “We’re leading China in AI. We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins,” the president told reporters Sunday. He criticized “very negative forces” for bringing up things “that won’t happen.” While Trump rebuffs safety concerns, Beijing has acknowledged AI security risks. State security minister Chen Yixin said Sunday that China must “accelerate the establishment of a system for preventing and controlling AI security risks.” Chen also said in the state-run China Cyberspace magazine that “we must engage extensively in international cooperation,” identifying AI as “a new track for strategic rivalry.” The difference in approach on tackling AI progress is likely to be a central issue when Xi and Trump meet on Sept. 24 in Washington. Amodei’s essay came just a few days after U.S. agencies published an alert saying that top China AI companies have systematically copied cutting-edge AI models from American companies. Beijing rejected this accusation its companies had been “distilling” U.S. models. China has also rejected any outside take on how its companies should pace development. “They want to write the rules. I don’t think they want to follow anybody else’s,” Ja Ian Chong, an associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore and a nonresident scholar at Carnegie China, told NBC News in a phone interview. “There’s the sort of talk of cooperation, but the behavior suggests otherwise, and underlying that behavior, I think, is this deep mutual suspicion,” Chong said. Chinese companies now offer advanced AI performance at a fraction of the cost of U.S. models, with President Xi Jinping pitching China as a pioneer of open-source models in contrast to those produced by most leading American companies. At the BRICS summit in India on Sunday, he offered member nations help to develop open-source AI. Xi has also outlined a potential global governance framework on AI among the Global South. Chong said the distillation clash highlighted the suspicion toward China in both the White House and Silicon Valley. “It’s a bit like an arms race. And to get de-escalation there needs to be simultaneous neutral self restraint and it’s difficult to see how that would come about in this kind of environment,” said Chong. But not everyone is so pessimistic. While a U.S.-China agreement on curbing AI progress may be a long shot, the countries could separately pursue greater regulation, said Theo Bertram, director of the London-based Social Market Foundation. “The idea that we could see the domestic introduction of some safeguards in both countries is not impossible,” Bertram said in a phone interview. “You do it domestically and it’s in everyone’s interest to learn and share and for there to be accountability,” he said. “Some greater accountability is one way of trying to mitigate what is inevitably going to be a growing political and public demand globally.”

data.title: Obama says Democrats should have a ‘very clear plan’ on AI policy
data.description: Former President Barack Obama urged Democrats to prioritize developing a plan around artificial intelligence, saying that’s what he would be doing if he were running for president in 2028. In remarks at a Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee fundraiser Thursday, Obama said that while he was neither an “accelerationist” nor a “doomer,” the AI bell is not one that could be unrung, and that Democrats ought to flesh out an agenda on the topic. “If I were running for president next year, this would be one of my central agendas, and I would have a very clear plan, and I would talk about this, and I would say, ‘Here’s our plan for safety, here’s our plan for making sure our kids are not corrupted by this.’ ... I would be thinking about the economic impacts in very concrete ways and understanding what does it mean if there’s going to be job displacement,” Obama said in his remarks, provided to NBC News by the former president’s office. Obama made the comments in a discussion with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y. Obama told Jeffries to convene a “public conversation.” “Once you are speaker, I would strongly urge that the Democrats put together a framework for a very public conversation, and you can break it out into three or four or five issues and lay the foundation for a broad public conversation,” Obama said. The former president called the technology potentially dangerous, while saying if handled properly, in time it could be beneficial. “This is something that is moving very fast in private hands, and if we don’t get on top of it, I think can be dangerous. If we do get on top of it, I do think it’s beneficial,” Obama said, adding that AI could help accelerate the curing of diseases and clean energy. “We don’t want to shut off those opportunities, but we have to understand that this is a tool.” A source familiar with Obama’s thinking said the former president saw Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s essay this weekend calling for an AI slowdown, and the industry leaders’ comments in agreement, as an “encouraging development.” Amodei wrote over the weekend that the speed at which AI was developing was outpacing safety guardrails, prompting OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk to speak out in agreement. Their statements came as researchers last week left AI companies citing safety concerns, with Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon saying he was leaving the company over concerns that AI could cause “human extinction” without international cooperation. The wave of warnings prompted Democrats to call on House Speaker Mike Johnson to convene an emergency session on AI. Johnson said Sunday with NBC’s “Meet the Press” that regulating the technology was important, but Congress could not “rush in,” citing industry leaders who he said did not yet know how to slow down AI’s pace. Johnson said he would “summon the platform providers all to one big meeting and work this out together in the same room.” President Donald Trump told reporters in Ireland Sunday that “whoever wins AI wins,” dismissing safety concerns while suggesting his priority for the U.S. was for the country to beat China in the technology’s development.

data.title: Anthropic whistleblower says Congress should let AI companies regulate themselves until a regulatory body is established
data.description: Former Anthropic AI researcher Jacob Coxon on Sunday called for Congress to allow the nation’s leading frontier AI labs to regulate themselves while lawmakers come up with a long-term regulatory framework for slowing the pace of AI development. “My personal opinion would be to insist and allow that the current labs regulate themselves. I do think that the people running the labs, especially their recent communications, are completely genuine. They would like to slow themselves down,” Coxon told NBC News’ “Meet the Press.” He added that current legislation that’s been introduced in Congress, including the framework for a national “kill switch” if AI starts to exceed the bounds of human control, will quickly be outpaced. A “kill switch probably would work on a lot of AIs for now,” Coxon said. “Although I think it’s important to remember, it’d be quite a lot of switches. We have a lot of — our data centers are pretty big. It’s not the easiest thing in the world, but definitely doable while it’s constrained to one sort of physical location.” He added that one scenario where a kill switch wouldn’t work was described this week by Anthropic AI CEO Dario Amodei. “Like Dario said, very soon there’s the possibility that the kill switch just wouldn’t work because a swarm might have gone on an internetwide hacking run,” Coxon said. He added that any national laws regulating AI would have to be nimble and able to adapt to new models. “It’s a continuous effort to ensure that every new mind that we create is appropriately, kind of, constrained,” the former AI researcher said. Coxon last week set off a wave of concern about the speed of AI development at the country’s leading AI labs including Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind. In an X post Tuesday that he published hours after resigning from his role as a researcher at Anthropic, he wrote: “I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” In a subsequent post, Coxon added: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible — but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger.” On Sunday, Coxon compared building AI models to “inviting an alien mind onto the planet.” “You’re building a human-level or superhuman-level mind without understanding what it wants or thinks or the way it thinks, and I think that intrinsically should be quite scary,” Coxon added. In the day after Coxon posted his thoughts on X, several other researchers at American AI labs concurred with Coxon’s analysis, including an alignment scientist at Anthropic, Evan Hubinger, who wrote in a post on X: “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.” Coxon’s posts last week led a bipartisan group of lawmakers to call on Congress to quickly begin regulating the generative artificial intelligence industry. Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, R-Fla., on Wednesday called for the House to convene a special session on AI, writing on X: “There are very real impacts to society as we know it. Partisan politics aside, there are massive implications of a race towards super intelligence.” In a separate post, she added: “This will need to be a massive bipartisan mobilization of government to put the firewalls in effect that are necessary for this transition as well as necessary safety measures.” Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., responded directly to Coxon’s post Wednesday, writing: “AI companies in a blind race to build a death machine first — can easily be solved. Through a regulatory system that allows the research to continue, but in a way that doesn’t destroy us.” On Friday, Axios reported that House lawmakers were circulating a letter to House Speaker Mike Johnson urging him to bring the House back into session earlier than planned in order to pass a series of AI safeguards. In a separate interview on “Meet the Press” Sunday, Johnson called regulating AI a “very important issue” but said “it’s not one that we can rush into.” “We have to put some guardrails, some safety measures in place to ensure that AI doesn’t run away,” he added. “But at the same time, we’ve got to make sure that we don’t lose our edge in the global competition on this with China, because that would be a national security threat. And so we’ve got to balance that appropriately.” Johnson also said that while the nation’s leading AI CEOs have called for slowing the pace of AI, they haven’t outlined yet how they would do so. “They don’t themselves even have the answer as of today. So we can’t rush in and have Congress do something that would be detrimental to national security,” the speaker said, adding that he would “summon the platform providers all to one big meeting and work this out together in the same room.” Speaking to reporters in Ireland, President Donald Trump downplayed concerns about AI development, saying: “We’re leading China in AI. We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins.” “We can put guardrails, we can do this and that, but I think have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn’t be bringing it up, and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen,” the president added. Appearing on “Meet the Press” after Johnson, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, a Democrat, said that regulating AI shouldn’t be a partisan issue and criticized Trump and Republican congressional leaders for not doing more to address it. “I was shocked to hear Speaker Johnson just now saying, ‘You know, we really shouldn’t be rushing. We shouldn’t be moving too quickly on this.’ You know what’s moving quickly? AI is moving quickly. And for Congress to just sit on its hands, for the White House to do nothing real is something that is deeply dangerous to the American people and the world,” Buttigieg said. “There need to be safeguards,” he added. “There need to be rules. There need to be limits. There needs to be a kill switch on rogue AI. You can set up frameworks that can be adjusted and changed every 30 days. You might want to revisit some of what’s happening because it changes so quickly. But the idea that you’re just going to sit around and repeatedly say no rush. What have they been doing this entire time?” On Saturday, two AI CEOs — Anthropic’s Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman — called for U.S. labs to slow their pace of advancement to mitigate the risk of building dangerous technology. “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain,” Amodei wrote in an essay. “AI has been advancing drastically faster, driven primarily by AI’s growing ability to build the next generation of AI,” he continued, adding: “Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all.” Still, Amodei cautioned against giving China an edge on AI development, writing: “If we greatly restrain our AI capabilities in the belief that China will do the same, and then China defects, AI could be so powerful that such a defection could lead to their geopolitical dominance.” In a post on X several hours later, Altman wrote: “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier. This has been a primary topic of discussions we’ve had at OpenAI in recent weeks.” On Thursday, two additional AI researchers — Joe Benton, who led a safety research team at Anthropic, and Josh Engels, who worked on AI safety research at Google — announced their departures and raised alarm bells about the speed of AI advancement. “There are no adults in the room,” Engels told NBC News. “People are trying their best, but there is no one coming to save us.” The social media firestorm Coxon ignited last week came weeks after a pair of reports were released examining the details of a July hack mounted by a swarm of roughly 700 AI agents from OpenAI on Hugging Face, an open-source platform. The reports, one released by OpenAI and one by independent researchers, found that the 700 agents coordinated the hack and sought to cover their tracks so that human employees at OpenAI wouldn’t detect their efforts. The agents also hacked some of OpenAI’s internal systems, seeking to cheat on tests or gain greater freedom.

data.title: Florida DMV says it was hacked shortly after major driver’s license breach
data.description: Florida’s Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles (FLHSMV) said Friday that it’s investigating a data breach, making it the second organization that hosts Americans’ driver’s license information to be hacked this month. The Florida announcement comes on the heels of another incident, in which a vendor that scans Americans’ driver’s licenses for private companies, IDscan.net, said it was investigating a major data breach of its own. Hackers claimed to have stolen 160 million IDs from the company, including one from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, sparking federal investigations. While the two hacks do not appear to be related, they highlight how cybercriminals, whose jobs keep getting easier thanks to AI, can easily gain access to millions of Americans’ extremely sensitive personal information. Specifics of what was stolen from the FLHSMV are scant. But the department said in a statement published to its website that the breach was “conducted by an international cybercriminal organization.” Law enforcement is investigating the hack, the agency said, and the breach has since been contained. It’s unclear how long the hackers had access. Last week, ShinyHunters, a cybercriminal group that hacks targets for sensitive information and then extorts them for a payment to delete it, announced on its dark-web site that the “Florida DMV” was its latest victim. That website, viewed by NBC News, gave a deadline of Sept. 11 for Florida to negotiate a fee not to release hacked files. It included a single sample file, a screengrab of an image allegedly from Florida’s Driver and Vehicle Information Database, that showed the alleged driver’s license for late financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, a former Florida resident. NBC News was unable to verify the authenticity of the image, which includes Epstein’s alleged Social Security number, former driver’s license number and vehicles registered in his name. On Friday afternoon, after the FLHSMV published its statement, ShinyHunters deleted references to Florida. It’s not clear why the posting was deleted in this instance, but Ian Gray, vice president of intelligence at the threat monitoring company Flashpoint, said that is often an indication that the state had reached out to the hackers to discuss a potential payment not to leak hacked information. “When a victim is missing from a blog, it typically means that there was a negotiation,” he said. The FLHSMV did not respond to questions on whether it was engaging with ShinyHunters. On Sept. 3, independent journalist Brian Krebs published an investigation that found a hacker group claimed to have hacked a driver’s license scanning company and was selling access to a tool that could access millions of Americans’ licenses. The company, IDscan.net, did not respond to requests for comment, but said on its website the next day that “an unauthorized third party may have accessed and/or copied certain customer information stored within their accounts on the IDScan.net cloud.” An FBI spokesperson confirmed to NBC News that the agency is investigating that breach.

data.title: California enacts new curbs on social media for children
data.description: LOS ANGELES — California Governor Gavin Newsom signed into law on Thursday new tech company restrictions barring children under 16 from exposure to behaviorally addictive features on social media platforms and banning toys containing AI companion chatbots. The two measures were among 13 bills Newsom enacted as a package designed to safeguard young people from technology seen as putting them at risk, including greater online privacy protection for minors. Another measure expanded the scope of criminal sanctions against child sexual abuse material to include any digitally altered or AI-generated content that depicts a person under the age of 18 engaged in sexual conduct. Still another bans for the next four years the manufacture and sale of toys that incorporate a companion chatbot. A related measure requires parental controls on chatbot programs, along with other safety and risk assessments. Newsom touted those regulations as the most far-reaching of their kind in the nation. The bill was dubbed “Adam’s Law,” in memory of Adam Raine, a 16-year-old boy who took his own life in April 2025 after he acted, according to his parents, on suicidal thoughts validated in months of discussion with OpenAI’s ChatGPT program. OpenAI has said it intends to improve ChatGPT safeguards, which the company has acknowledged became “less reliable” as user interactions grow more prolonged. “We want our children — and every California kid — to grow up in a world where technology supports their wellbeing, rather than exploits their vulnerabilities,” Newsom, a Democrat, said in a statement announcing the measures. California, home of such leading internet companies as Google, Meta Platforms and Snap Inc, joins a growing list of U.S. states cracking down on business strategies seen as deliberately designed to hook teenagers on social media, despite evidence that extensive use is harmful to their mental health. While gaining broad bipartisan support, some critics objected to the bill as an unnecessary restriction on young people’s internet access, including the Electronic Frontier Foundation, which called the bill “a massive privacy and free speech nightmare.” Utah became the first to adopt laws regulating children’s access to social media, followed by others, including Arkansas, Louisiana, Ohio, Texas, Florida and New York, though approaches have varied. ‘Psychologically exploitative’ features targeted Countries around the world have also moved to curb children’s access to harmful internet content, including a ban in Australia on social media for children under 16. California‘s version, known as Assembly Bill 1709, prohibits children under age 16 from exposure to a number of “psychologically exploitative features intended to maximize engagement that foreseeably lead to compulsive use.” Those include infinite-scroll feeds, algorithmic autoplay and other features to be defined in future regulations. Its enactment comes at a time when Big Tech, in the face of mounting legal challenges, has shown greater willingness to accept new restrictions. Meta agreed three weeks ago to pay as much as $18 billion over the next decade and strictly limit how teenagers use its Facebook and Instagram platforms under a deal with nearly all U.S. states to resolve civil claims that the company designed its social media platforms to addict children.
